card.front: In authentication, authorisation and accounting, what is accounting?
card.back: Recording what a user is doing or has done.
card.explanation: It usually follows authentication and authorisation, and its records serve as an auditing tool for security or to charge for the services used.
card.example: Like a building’s visitor log noting who went into which room and for how long, after the guard has checked their pass.
card.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

reason: Seven cards in topics 19 and 21 use “accounting” before any primer; isc2-cc lists the term but never teaches it. RFC 8907 §7: “Accounting is the action of recording what a user is doing and/or has done.”

value: A server that relays one application’s traffic, such as email or web, as a proxy, with much more limited firewalling than an application-proxy gateway.
reason: The back defined a proxy server only by contrast, so a newcomer never learnt what it does. SP 800-41r1 p. 16–17: proxy control of traffic, limited firewalling, hand off to “the appropriate proxy server (e.g., email proxy)”.

value: CASBs show which cloud services staff use, curbing unauthorised cloud use, and today’s CASBs also extend on-premises security policies to cloud applications.
reason: The stem asks for data rules on approved cloud apps, but the explanation covered only discovery. SP 800-215 p. 17: “The current generation of CASBs enforces security and governance policies for cloud applications, thus enabling enterprises to extend their on-premises policies to the cloud.”

value: Without 802.1X, everyone joining the network authenticates with the same pre-shared key.
reason: SP 800-77r1 p. 104 says only that Enterprise versions use 802.1X instead of a PSK; it never names “Personal versions”.

value: A: nobody is denying having sent a message. B: nothing is disclosed to anyone. D: nothing is altered. NIST links a high volume of spam to availability.
reason: “Nothing here is disclosed, altered or denied by a sender” packed three distractors into one clause that has to be read twice.

value: Why does adversarial machine learning count model extraction as a privacy attack?
reason: The old front re-taught cc.ai-security-across-the-domains.privacy-compromise (privacy covers confidentiality); reworked to build on it.

value: Its term “privacy” covers attacks on a model’s confidentiality, such as extracting its weights or architecture, as well as exposure of training data.
reason: Follows the new front; AI 100-2 E2025 p. 20.

value: The field says “privacy” where traditional security taxonomies say “confidentiality”, so taking information about the model itself falls under it.
reason: Follows the new front.
